Nearly all covariates are associated with cognitive performance S7 and S9). These associations reflect the covariation between covariates and cognitive outcomes after accounting for adversity exposures, and should not be interpreted as direct or causal effects given the observational nature of our data. There are negative associations among age and environmental noise during the experiment with working memory capacity: older individuals and individuals who experience a noisy environment during cognitive testing tend to show worse working memory capacity. There is a positive association between income-to-needs ratio and working memory updating, such that individuals from higher socioeconomic strata tend to show better working memory updating. Similarly, there are positive associations between education and working memory capacity and executive functioning information processing: individuals who completed higher education, tend to show better working memory capacity and more efficient general information processing. Unexpectedly, there are consistent negative associations among education and working memory updating: individuals with lower education tend to show better working memory updating. Notably, all these associations are partly mediated through our adversity exposure variables. This means that adversity may account for some, but not all, of the observed covariation between sociodemographic characteristics and cognitive performance. With the exception of sex in the working memory health models, the depicted covariates were consistently significant across all models. Note that the income-to-needs ratio is only included in the scarcity models. For sex, we coded females as 1 and males as 0.

Discussion

This study tracked individuals and their environments over approximately a decade, combining self-reported measures from the LISS panel with administrative records from CBS registers to examine associations between adversity and cognition. Across both the executive functioning and working memory samples, we find that self-report and registry-based adversity measures are only moderately correlated, replicating patterns documented in the broader literature 13, 22, 36, [49] [50] [51] [52] . Critically, although associations with administrative and selfreport measures converged for some cognitive outcomes, they diverged for others. Patterns of convergence and divergence differed across cognitive outcomes. For working memory capacity, self-reported and administrative neighborhood threat showed opposite associations (a same-construct, data-source-dependent reversal). For executive functioning, the divergence occurred across adversity dimensions: administrative unpredictability was positively associated with information processing, while self-reported neighborhood threat was negatively associated. These two patterns are related but distinct, and we discuss them accordingly below. Additionally, many of the associations between adversity measures (both self-report and administrative) and executive functioning parameters fell within the region of practical equivalence (intact cognitive performance). Below we discuss what these convergent and divergent patterns reveal about how adversity is measured, experienced, and linked to cognition.

At the heart of our study is the comparison of self-report (LISS) and administrative (CBS) data. Across both samples, self-report measures tend to correlate more strongly with other self-report measures than with administrative measures, and vice versa. This suggests that the two data sources form partially distinct measurement clusters. These findings are consistent with prior work documenting poor agreement between self-reported and administrative measures of adversity, and with the conclusion that they identify partially distinct groups at risk for worse outcomes 15 . Further linking our adversity measures to cognition, we find stronger associations (as indexed by the absolute standardized effect) with self-reported adversity measures compared to administrative measures, irrespective of cognitive outcome.

Thus, our results deviate from prior work reporting that perceptions of adversity were more strongly related to attention shifting, whereas objective measures were more strongly related to working memory 61 . One important difference between this work and our study is that the objective measures were derived from structured interviews (e.g. tabulating the number of moves), thereby still being self-reported. Although smaller in magnitude, we also observe significant associations between cognitive outcomes and administrative records. However, the direction of these associations is sometimes opposite of those observed for self-report measures. Specifically, we find that self-reported neighborhood threat and the self-report adversity composite are negatively associated with both working memory capacity and general information processing, potentially in line with a deficit pattern. Further aligning with these patterns, we observe a negative association between administrative crime victimization and information processing. In contrast, administrative neighborhood threat is positively associated with working memory capacity, and administrative unpredictability in crime rates is positively associated with information processing, potentially consistent with performance enhancements. Importantly, the positive association with unpredictability and the negative association with self-reported neighborhood threat reflect divergence between different adversity dimensions for information processing, not a same-construct reversal across data sources as for working memory capacity. Together, these findings suggest that the relationship between adversity and cognition is complex: the data source, adversity dimension, and cognitive outcome can all moderate the direction and magnitude of associations. However, we note that our significant associations with administrative adversity measures show small effect sizes that only just fall outside the practical equivalence band of ±0.10, highlighting the need for replication.

At the same time, we find that many adversity associations fall within the region of practical equivalence, particularly for CBS-derived administrative neighborhood threat and LISS selfreported health issues in the executive functioning sample. One possibility is that adversity does not affect brain function and structure in a way that impacts these cognitive abilities, even though it may alter underlying processes [53] [54] [55] . Alternatively, intact performance might reflect a combination of impairment and adaptive processes, where impairment processes generally lower cognition, while adaptive processes boost certain relevant abilities (the net effect being intact performance), but not other abilities (thus, lower performance) 57 . Either way, intact performance is inconsistent with a deficit perspective alone, which predicts negative associations with adversity.

Our application of unpredictability statistics to longitudinal administrative crime data is a novel contribution. The predominantly positive associations among unpredictability indices are consistent with prior work applying this framework to other data sources, supporting the validity of the approach 44 . The exception (not computed in that prior work)-entropy's consistent negative associations with other indices-implies that our residential crime time series are likely either characterized by infrequent, abrupt spikes combined with low variability, or by high, sustained, chronic variability. In a sensitivity analysis (see methods), the significant positive association between unpredictability and information processing remained even after removing entropy from the construct. From this we infer that the association is not driven by entropy and that, in our sample, chronic variability in crime rates experienced at the neighborhood level may weigh more heavily than episodic, abrupt disruptions. This positive association between unpredictability and general information processing is predicted neither by adaptation frameworks nor by deficit frameworks, and warrants replication 66 . Importantly, this effect was sensitive to preprocessing decisions, particularly the imputation of zeros, which artificially stabilized some time series and reversed the association. This sensitivity underscores the importance of transparent reporting of preprocessing choices in unpredictability research, and points to the need for further methodological work on how to handle missing data in time series data.

We further observe consistent indirect associations among covariates and cognitive outcomes across models, which replicate well-established findings. Age-related decline in working memory capacity and the positive association between education and information processing are well-supported in previous research [67] [68] [69] . The positive association between income-toneeds ratio and working memory updating is consistent with a large literature linking socioeconomic status to executive functioning [70] [71] [72] . More surprising are the consistent negative associations between education and working memory updating across models. This pattern warrants cautious interpretation given the correlational nature of these associations. It is possible that unmeasured confounders, or confounders we could not measure precisely enough, are responsible for this negative association rather than a true underlying relationship.

Comparing individual-and neighborhood-level adversity measures, we find that associations with cognitive outcomes mainly occur for neighborhood-level measures, or for those which include neighborhood-level indicators (administrative neighborhood threat, administrative unpredictability in neighborhood threat, self-reported neighborhood threat, self-reported adversity composite). These findings replicate previous work in these samples 8, 45 . However, as noted above, while self-reported neighborhood adversity measures tend to be negatively associated with cognitive outcomes, the opposite is true for administrative measures (except for crime victimization). These results contrast with a growing body of research linking objective neighborhood deprivation indices to lower working memory and executive function performance in adulthood, with effects persisting after adjustment for individual-level socioeconomic status 73 . Our findings add nuance to this picture. It is not simply that objective neighborhood adversity impairs cognition; rather, the nature of the adversity measure matters.

Individual crime victimization-a more direct and proximal form of adversity that may or may not occur at the neighborhood level-was associated with less efficient information processing (a performance deficit), whereas exposure to higher average crime rates across residential histories was associated with better working memory capacity (a performance enhancement). This result may be consistent with an adaptationist perspective: sustained exposure to threatening environments may adaptively tailor cognitive abilities to environmental demands, while direct victimization may carry costs that outweigh any such functional benefits. However, we emphasize that this adaptationist account is one of several post-hoc explanations for a pattern not predicted a priori by either the deficit or adaptation frameworks.

An equally parsimonious account is residential selection: cognitively or economically advantaged individuals may differentially select into, or be better able to leave, higher-crime neighborhoods for reasons not fully captured by education and income-toneeds. Our cross-sectional outcome assessment precludes distinguishing environmental effects from selection effects, and we treat the adaptationist interpretation as hypothesisgenerating rather than supported.

Zooming out, our main result, the observed divergence between associations with self-reports and administrative records, suggests that both sources may index meaningfully different aspects of adversity exposure. Self-reports often capture individuals' perceptions of their environment, which are shaped by appraisal and affective response. Administrative records, by contrast, capture the objective exposure to adversity, irrespective of how that exposure is experienced. These insights dovetail with contemporary discussions about the importance of distinguishing between objectively experienced and subjectively perceived adversity 11, 74 . We acknowledge that the broader thesis, that objective experiences and subjective perceptions can have different outcomes, is well-established in health and developmental psychopathology 15, 22, 36 . Our contribution is to extend this question to adult cognition, where the literature contrasting self-report and administrative measures is sparse. The sameconstruct reversal we observe for working memory capacity is, to our knowledge, novel in this domain, though the effect size is modest and replication is needed before strong conclusions can be drawn. But how does the same neighborhood put individuals on different trajectories of meaning-making and perceptions of neighborhood threat? One contributing factor is individuals' mental health, which can color their perceptions and interpretation of adverse experiences. Previous work found, for example, that mental health was more strongly predicted by subjective neighborhood perceptions, whereas physical and social health outcomes were more strongly predicted by objective neighborhood features 75 . Although our study did not include mental health, it is possible that individuals' mental health mediated the negative association between self-reported neighborhood threat and cognitive outcomes reported here. To test this possibility, future work could extend the present study by incorporating mental health and other physical outcome measures to better understand the diverging effects between self-report and administrative adversity measures.

Our study contributes to an ongoing debate about how adversity should be operationalized.

On the one hand, cumulative risk approaches advocate for 'lumping' diverse adversities into a single index. On the other hand, dimensional models 'split' adversity into dimensions, such as deprivation, threat, and unpredictability which may have distinct associations with neural and cognitive development 11, 76, 77 . Our results can inform both of these approaches. The selfreport adversity composite (a singular index) shows a negative association with cognition, suggesting that cumulative perceived adversity carries cognitive costs. Notably, only one of the individual self-report adversity measures showed a significant negative association with the same outcome. Examining the CBS composite measure, we find no association between cumulative administrative adversity and cognition. Yet, our individual measures did reveal significant associations, and moreover, not all adversity measures pointed in the same direction: administrative neighborhood threat was associated with enhanced working memory performance and the administrative crime victimization with lowered performance. Lumping these together would not only obscure this divergence, but in our case even entirely hide the association between administrative adversity measures and cognition.

Recent work 11, 74, 78 argues that both lumping and splitting have limitations, calling for frameworks that attend to how adversity is experienced and interpreted by the individual. We have taken initial steps towards such a framework by combining longitudinal administrative data with self-reported perceptions within the same individuals. Our finding that objective exposure and subjective perception of the same adversity dimension (neighborhood threat) are associated with cognitive outcomes in opposite directions may be the clearest illustration of why this distinction matters. The same neighborhood, objectively characterized by high crime rates, might be experienced as threatening and cognitively taxing by one individual, while another-perhaps someone who has developmentally adapted to that environment across years of residence-may show no such cognitive costs, or even strengths.

Our study has five main limitations. The first concerns scope, specifically generalizability across contexts and ages. We have studied a generalizable Dutch sample. However, it is an open question to what extent our findings generalize to other cultures and countries, including those that do not include universal schooling (e.g. from rural communities) 79 . Additionally, as our measurement period excludes childhood, there is a question about the generalizability across development. Previous work has shown that the associations between adversity and cognition may differ in magnitude and direction depending on the developmental period during which adversity is experienced 31 . Second, administrative data are not perfectly objective. They can be influenced by various types of selection and reporting biases at the geographical level (e.g. which acts get reported) and the individual level (e.g. who gets investigated) 80, 81 . Third, while our use of residential histories to derive neighborhood-level crime indicators is a methodological advance, actual exposure to neighborhood crime is not fully captured by residential location alone: mobility within neighborhoods, time spent outside the home, and social networks all shape effective exposure. Fourth, the moderate correlations between LISS and CBS measures, while consistent with prior literature, also mean that neither source fully captures the respective adversity dimension. Fifth, our crosssectional outcome assessment precludes causal inference. In particular, the associations we find are compatible both with selection effects (individuals with higher cognitive ability selecting into different neighborhoods) and with environmental effects (experienced conditions influencing cognitive performance). Longitudinal designs with repeated cognitive assessments, or quasi-experimental designs exploiting exogenous variation in neighborhood assignment (e.g. Moving to Opportunity study 35 ), are needed to disentangle selection from environmental effects. We therefore caution against interpreting the positive administrative associations as evidence of cognitive enhancement caused by adversity exposure.

Our findings highlight four crucial directions for future research. First, the divergent patterns across data sources call for studies that explicitly model the gap between objective exposure and subjective perception as a variable of interest in its own right: individuals who perceive their environment as more threatening than objective indicators may be particularly at risk for worse outcomes. Second, life-course modeling approaches that use the full temporal structure of administrative records could reveal whether the timing of adversity exposure, not just its cumulative level, moderates cognitive outcomes, thus providing insights into sensitive periods for adversity exposure 82, 83 . Third, extending our present study to include childhood measures would allow us to explore whether adversity-cognition associations reflect developmental adaptation or adult-stage processes. Finally, the unpredictability framework 38 applied to neighborhood crime could be extended to other administrative time series (e.g. income, health issues) to build a richer, multi-domain picture of environmental unpredictability across the lifespan.

In conclusion, our study shows that self-report and administrative adversity measures capture distinct facets of individuals' lived experiences, and that these facets are associated with cognitive outcomes in different, sometimes opposing, directions. Perceived adversity is associated with lower cognitive performance, and objective exposure to neighborhood crime is sometimes associated with performance enhancements, particularly in working memory capacity. These findings underscore the value of combining subjective and objective measures within the same individuals across time. Our results echo recent calls for theoretical frameworks that can accommodate the possibility that the same environmental conditions carry different cognitive consequences depending on how they are experienced 11, 74, 78.

Data availability and access

LISS raw data are publicly available to researchers through the LISS archive (https://www.lissdata.nl/how-it-works-archive). The data and code repositories of the two previous publications describe how the data from the LISS archive can be downloaded and prepared (https://stefanvermeent.github.io/liss_wm_profiles_2023/ and https://stefanvermeent.github.io/liss_ef_2024/). While the cognitive measures are the same as in those publications, we adjusted the independent variables to match the current year range (2013-2022/2023). Additionally, the previous two studies merged neighborhood threat variables and crime experiences into a violence composite.
